observation_summary: The compiler fails to correctly resolve qualified names (e.g., 'ns.foo') when they are declared within a local scope but intended to be global, leading to incorrect type inference and scope management.
hypothesis: The scope resolution logic in TypedScopeCreator incorrectly restricts the declaration of qualified names to the current local scope, even when they are rooted in the global scope. The fix introduces a check to promote the declaration of such names to the global scope if they are not already declared there.
prediction: The code will now correctly identify that a qualified name like 'ns.foo' should be associated with the global scope when it is first encountered, preventing subsequent type check failures.
experiment_rationale: The fix adds a conditional check (if GETPROP and not global scope) to re-target the scope of declaration to the global scope. This is a procedural change to the scope resolution algorithm, not a design-level capability addition or a simple value assignment.
reasoning_summary: The bug is a procedural error in how the compiler determines the scope for qualified names. The fix modifies the logic (the algorithm) used to decide which scope a variable should be declared in. It is not a missing check (Checking), not a wrong constant (Assignment/Initialization), and not a design-level capability gap (Function/Class/Object). It is a refinement of the existing scope resolution method.

alternative_types.why_not_primary: While the fix adds a conditional check, the purpose is to change the procedural outcome (scope assignment) rather than just validating input.
This is a local procedural fix within the scope resolution logic, not a design-level capability correction.
